Reality check: healthcare costs aren’t skyrocketing because of Republicans or Donald Trump.
They’re exploding because of structural failures that both parties allowed to metastasize for decades.

The real root causes:
https://t.co/07rnOILnxd consolidation & private equity
•Community hospitals are closing because large hospital systems and PE firms buy them, load them with debt, cut staff, and jack up prices.
•Fewer competitors = higher prices. That’s not ideology, it’s economics.
2.Administrative bloat
•The U.S. healthcare system spends hundreds of billions a year on billing, coding, compliance, and insurance bureaucracy.
•Hospitals now employ more administrators than doctors. That cost gets passed straight to patients.
3.Third-party payer distortion
•When insurers and government programs negotiate behind closed doors, prices become fictional.
•Providers inflate “chargemaster” prices to survive under Medicare/Medicaid underpayments, and privately insured patients get crushed to make up the gap.
4.Unfunded mandates
•Emergency rooms are legally required to treat everyone, regardless of ability to pay.
•That’s morally right—but when government reimbursement doesn’t cover costs, hospitals either close or shift the bill to everyone else.
5.Regulatory capture
•Certificate-of-Need laws and restrictive licensing block new hospitals, clinics, and surgical centers from opening.
•Less supply, more demand, higher prices. Again—math, not politics.
6.Aging population + chronic disease
•Longer lifespans and preventable chronic illness (diabetes, obesity, heart disease) drive sustained cost growth.
•No politician caused biology.

What’s misleading about the original claim
•Community health centers are filling gaps created by system failure, not partisan policy.
•Healthcare costs were rising long before Trump, and continued rising after Trump.
•Hospital closures are highest in states with heavy regulation and low reimbursement, not based on who controls Congress.

The honest conclusion

Healthcare isn’t “being decimated” by one party.
It’s being suffocated by consolidation, bureaucracy, distorted incentives, and bad economics that neither side wanted to confront.

If we actually want lower costs and better access, the focus should be on:
•Price transparency
•Competition
•Reduced administrative waste
•Fair reimbursement
•Breaking up monopolistic hospital systems

That’s not radical. That’s adult problem-solving.
